title: The giant in the fog
told: from the life of Carl Jung

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there someone who gets under your skin more than they probably should?
options: keep them in mind. no blame, just curiosity.
that’s most of us. watch what jung noticed.
lucky you. keep this one for when it happens.

steps.line: In Switzerland, a young man named Carl Jung, who would become a famous psychiatrist, had a dream he never forgot.
It was night. He was pushing against a mighty wind through thick fog, his hands cupped around a tiny light that might go out at any moment.

steps.q: He turns, and a gigantic black figure is right behind him. What do you think he does?
steps.why: Terrified, he knew he had to keep his little light going, he wrote, through night and wind, whatever happened.

steps.line: He looked back and saw a gigantic black figure following him. Afraid, he kept walking, still protecting the little light.

steps.q: He wakes up. What does he realize the giant was?
o: A warning about a real enemy
His own shadow, cast by his light
steps.why: His own shadow, thrown huge onto the fog by the light he was carrying.

steps.line: When he woke, he understood. The giant was his own shadow, thrown onto the fog by the little light he carried.

steps.q: Why does it matter that the shadow came from his own light?
o: Any light you carry casts a shadow
So the shadow wasn’t really there
He should put the light out
steps.why: You can’t have the light without the shadow. Jung took that as the deal of seeing at all: the more you see, the more you notice what follows you.

steps.line: Years later, Jung used the word shadow for the parts of ourselves we’d rather not claim. Not only dark ones. Hidden gifts, too.

steps.pre: Jung wrote that the little light was his
steps.why: Consciousness: his power to see and know himself. A light like that lets you see, and it casts a shadow too.

steps.line: Today, it’s called shadow work. Minus the jargon, it’s one question when someone bugs you more than they should: is any of this mine?
steps.label: today

steps.q: What did Jung say a person should do with their shadow?
o: Defeat it and drive it out
Get to know it, and take it back
steps.why: Jung’s word was integration: owning what you’d pushed away. He aimed at wholeness, not perfection.

say: here’s what i love. jung didn’t think you could get rid of your shadow. you carry a light, you cast one. his aim was to become whole, not perfect.
so the work is gentle: notice what bugs you, and ask if a piece of it lives in you. and for old, heavy pain, a good therapist is the right company.

steps.q: Jung wrote that you don’t become enlightened by imagining figures of light. What did he say instead?
o: By letting the darkness pass by
steps.why: From his essay “The Philosophical Tree” (1945). Not chasing the dark away, and not ignoring it: bringing it into the light you carry.

today.say: today, when someone bugs you, try one line in your notes: their name, the trait in one word, and the gentle question, is any of this mine?
options: gently does it. no verdict needed.
that counts. you know the question now.

card.from: from the life of Carl Jung
card.keepWhy: Carry the light. Own the shadow.
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962; English trans. Richard and Clara Winston, 1963), chapter “Student Years”: the dream of walking at night against a mighty wind in dense fog, hands cupped around a tiny light; a gigantic black figure following; on waking he realized it was a “specter of the Brocken,” his own shadow on the swirling mists, cast by the little light, and that the light was his consciousness.
Jung on the shadow and projection: e.g. Aion (1951), chapter 2, “The Shadow”; Collected Works vol. 9ii.
The shadow is not wholly bad and holds good qualities too: e.g. Psychology and Religion (1938), Collected Works vol. 11, §134.
Right after the dream, the memoir reads it through his personalities No. 1 (the bearer of the light) and No. 2 (following like a shadow).
